name: Copper Brown
lede: Copper Brown is a dark reddish brown, a name that in nineteenth-century pigment lists meant a brown made from copper compounds, not the color of the metal.

sections.title: A pigment name
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium records copper brown as a name listed by the color-maker Salter in 1869 and says it apparently refers to copper hexacyanoferrate(II) and other unspecified copper compounds [1]. The Colour Index gives a second recipe, numbered CI 77403, that starts from copper sulfate and magnesium sulfate [1]. The first compound belongs to the hexacyanoferrate group, the same group as [[prussian-blue]] [2].

The same family of copper compounds collected other names over time: Hatchett's brown, copper brown and Vandyke red [2]. Historically, then, the word named a family of obscure laboratory browns, and the entry gives no sign that painters relied on it.

sections.title: The swatch is a system color
sections.body: The swatch is not a recreation of that pigment. It comes from the ISCC-NBS 1955 list, block 55, and from the RAL (1927) and Maerz and Paul charts, and the nearest ISCC-NBS name is "moderate reddish brown", 4.4 units away [3]. It sits between [[russet]] and [[umber]] in warmth.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive it appears in 1,922 of 23,781 paintings, 8.08 per cent, and is commoner than 91 per cent of named colors [4]. Inside a painting it is most often an accent, in 63 per cent of the 1,108 paintings where it counts [4]. It peaks in the 1300s, at 7.6 per cent of 251 paintings, 1.9 times the museums' baseline [4]. Cornelius Norbertus Gijsbrechts is the most devoted painter, with it in 5 of his 19 works here [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a color, not a pigment test [4].
